"The <term>Vetala</term> <gloss>spirit residing in a corpse</gloss> gave me human flesh to eat for satisfaction. I consumed it immediately, and as I was satisfied, the one hungry for human flesh said to me: 'Bring nothing else.'" 49

"When I could no longer endure the time, I cut off my own flesh and offered it to him. The <term>Yogeshvara</term> <gloss>master of yoga</gloss> was pleased with me for that." 50

"Then he said to me: 'Friend, I am now pleased with your firm resolve. Therefore, be as you were before, with an uninjured body, and choose the boon you desire from me.'" 51

"When he said this, I replied to him at that very moment: 'Lead me, O God, to the place where my lord <term>Mrigankadatta</term> is. No other boon is desired by me than this.'" 52

"Hearing this, the Lord of the <term>Vetalas</term> said to me: 'Then climb upon my back, and I will quickly carry you to that lord of the sky.'" 53

"When he spoke thus, I agreed, and having quickly climbed onto his shoulders, he took me through the path of the sky, having entered the corpse." 54

"Having brought me here and seeing you all, he set me down from the sky on the road. O Lord, by this great <term>Vetala</term>, I have been brought to your feet." 55

"I have reached my lord, and he, having completed his task, has gone. This is the great story, O giver of honor, of my being freed from the serpent's snare." 56

The account of the separation having been heard from his own minister by <term>Vikramakesari</term>, the Prince <term>Mrigankadatta</term>, as he went along the road to <term>Ujjayini</term> for the sake of his beloved, rejoiced. 57

That Prince, having gathered a few of his followers who had become separated due to the shifting of the army, rejoiced, considering all his objectives possible of attainment. 58

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the <term>Shashankavati Lambaka</term> <gloss>section named after the princess Shashankavati</gloss> of the <term>Kathasaritsagara</term> <gloss>Ocean of the Streams of Stories</gloss>, composed by the great poet, the illustrious <term>Somadevabhatta</term>.

The Thirty-third Chapter.

Salutation to the conqueror of obstacles <note>Ganesha</note>, whose knee serves as the pot for the constellation of stars that revolve as he dances in the night. 1

Then, at the end of the story, <term>Mrigankadatta</term>, having risen from the middle of the road, was joyful to have found <term>Vikramakesari</term>. 2

Accompanied by <term>Gunakara</term>, as well as <term>Vimalabuddhi</term>, with his wondrous tales and endowed with immense prowess. 3

Together with <term>Prachandashakti</term> and accompanied by the Brahmin <term>Shrutadhi</term>, he began searching for the remaining companions who had been separated by the curse. 4

Having already set out toward <term>Ujjayini</term> for the sake of <term>Shashankavati</term>, he started on his journey again, himself being the eighth. 5

Gradually, he reached a forest in the <term>Bhima</term> region, where the water had dried up, and the sand was scorched by the heat of the fierce sun. 6

Walking in that forest, the Prince spoke to those ministers: "Look at this forest, how difficult to traverse and how terrifyingly vast." 7

"It is a place without water, lacking people, and without shelter, as if it were the rising flames of the fire at the end of time, shimmering with desert mirages." 8

"With its dry and tangled brushwood that rustles, and thorns that cause the hair to stand on end from the fear of lions, tigers, and other beasts." 9

"It seems to be weeping with the cries of deer longing for water at the end of the dry season. Therefore, this vast and difficult place must be crossed by us with speed." 10

Having said this, <term>Mrigankadatta</term> quickly crossed that forest with his ministers, who were afflicted by hunger and thirst. 11

And ahead, he saw a very large lake with clear, cool water, like the liquid moon-nectar melted by the heat of the sun. 12

<summary>Mrigankadatta is reunited with his minister Vikramakesari, who recounts his survival and the favor of the Vetala. The prince and his seven companions then continue their journey toward Ujjayini, crossing a treacherous and parched desert forest until they discover a life-saving lake.</summary>
<keywords>Mrigankadatta, Vikramakesari, Vetala, Ujjayini, Shashankavati, journey, desert, reunion</keywords>
